S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. These experiences are time-consuming or cause marked distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and the individual typically recognizes that the thoughts and behaviors are excessive or unreasonable. The course is often chronic with waxing and waning intensity, frequently exacerbated by stress, transitions, or increased responsibility. OCD is distinguished from psychotic disorders by preserved reality testing and from generalized anxiety by the presence of specific, ritualized thoughts or behaviors rather than diffuse, free-floating worry.

patient.stressor: Sarah had managed a demanding career in community analytics for decades by relying on detailed project plans, version control, and careful quality checks that colleagues admired as thoroughness. Two years ago, her organization underwent a restructuring that expanded her responsibilities, placing her in charge of multiple high‑visibility data initiatives with tight deadlines and public scrutiny from city officials and community groups. Under this pressure, her need to feel certain about every dataset and model output intensified, and she began spending longer and longer hours re‑reviewing work, falling behind on timelines, and avoiding delegating to junior staff because she feared missing something crucial. When she found herself skipping salsa nights, turning down hikes, and staying late in the office repeatedly to re‑open completed analyses, her manager raised concerns about project delays and she noticed her usual coping routines no longer worked; after a particularly tense stakeholder meeting where she froze over worries about having made an unseen mistake, she contacted her primary care physician, who referred her for a psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m stuck double‑ and triple‑checking my analyses for hours, even when I know they’re done, and it’s starting to derail my projects.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: Lately my brain latches onto these horrible what‑if thoughts, like what if I made a tiny error in a dataset that leads to the city making a bad policy decision, and even when I know the numbers are right I can’t shut off the replay of worst‑case scenarios long enough to focus on anything else.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: When I finish an analysis, I’ll find myself going back through the code, the formulas, and the exports over and over—sometimes for hours—re-running the same checks or scrolling line by line, because I feel this intense need to be absolutely certain I didn’t miss some hidden mistake, even though I’m already late on the deadline and I know it doesn’t make sense to keep checking.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: Over the past year or so, I’ve started missing project deadlines, getting called into meetings about my productivity, and turning down social plans because I stay late at the office re-checking work instead of actually finishing it.
